newsitem.title: USA: ICI chmn says bear market won't slow fund growth.
newsitem.headline: ICI chmn says bear market won't slow fund growth.

text.p: Total mutual fund assets will keep growing, even if U.S. stocks suffer through a bear market next year, the new chairman of the Investment Company Institute predicted.
"Even in a bear market, it's going to continue to grow," Don Powell told Reuters in an interview. "I don't see the industry going into net redemptions. So much of the cash flow is automatic."
Powell declined to issue a specific forecast.
Powell, president and chief executive officer of Van Kampen American Capital Inc, referred to the steady flow of defined contribution -- or pension -- money into mutual funds.
At the end of August, the pension industry had about $3.2 trillion in assets invested in equity, fixed-income and money-market funds.
Powell was elected last week as chairman of the ICI, the U.S. mutual fund trade group, replacing Jon Fossel.
Powell said about 35 percent of total assets are in pension plans, and that the ICI estimated the same percentage of cash was flowing into mutual funds from those sources.
Powell said he did not expect fund flows to maintain the same levels as in the first half of 1996. In January, the flow into stock funds reached $28.93 billion.
"I suspect it was a bit of a spike," he said. "We just had a phenomenal run in equity funds."
He expects the current lack of interest in fixed-income funds will change, especially in tax-free money-market funds, if the U.S. moves closer to a flat income tax.
He also said he expected the trend of industry consolidation to continue.
The industry is oversaturated, he said, with about 400 open-end fund companies selling more than 6,100 funds.
"That strikes me as very excessive," he said. "I think it's confusing now. It's an overwhelming number of products for people to understand."
"I think it's just impossible for brokers or the public to keep track of the number of vendors of mutual funds," he added. "You need to be large to succeed in this business."
Powell sees bigger firms gobbling up those with less than $10 billion in assets as the costs of marketing and distribution keep rising.
He said mergers between small firms were less likely, as such deals would not solve cost and distribution problems.
Powell considers consolidation as beneficial for both the industry and investors.
"We'll end up with the industry in very strong hands," he said. "You'll end up with players who have scale and mass, the kinds of people who have shareholder interests in mind."
Powell said he thought that either a Clinton and Dole administration would have a favourable view of the ICI's goal of privatizing a portion of the U.S. Social Security program.

"It's become kind of a bipartisan issue," he said. "Everybody is beginning to realize that we're going to have to do something to fix Social Security sooner or later. The longer we wait, the harder it will be to fix."
Powell backs a plan to allow individuals to control the investment of a portion of the 12.4 percent that the government withholds for Social Security.
Powell said one of the main problems facing the industry is educating investors. "An informed and educated public is probably the one (problem) I am most seriously worried about," he said.
He said investors often buy funds without completely understanding the risks and returns they can expect.
"We have 38 million shareholders," he said. "I would like for those people to understand what they're buying, and the kinds of investments they are making."
